groups.name: The Law or the Pentateuch
groups.description: About creation and the history of mankind before and after the flood; the origin of the nations and of Israel; and the Law and covenant God gave them. Jews call these five books the Torah ('instruction'); tradition names Moses as their author.

books.name: Genesis
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Bereshit, 'In the beginning' (its first word). The Greek title Genesis means 'origin'.
books.summary: The book of beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood, the nations, and God's covenant family from Abraham to Joseph.
books.author: Moses (traditional)
books.author_note: Jewish and Christian tradition, and Jesus himself ('the law of Moses', Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Moses is recorded writing parts of it (Exodus 24:4; Deuteronomy 31:9). Many modern scholars see it as compiled from several sources over centuries and completed around the exile; conservative scholars hold to Mosaic authorship with later editorial touches such as the account of Moses' death.
books.date: c. 1446–1406 BC by the traditional dating; final form debated
books.audience: Israel in the wilderness, about to enter Canaan
books.setting: From creation to Joseph's death in Egypt (patriarchal age, c. 2000–1800 BC traditionally)
books.origin: Genesis gave Israel its story before Sinai: where the world, sin, death and the nations came from, and why God chose one family. It weaves genealogies ('these are the generations of…', ten times) with narratives that ancient Israel treasured, and echoes and answers Near Eastern creation and flood stories with a single, good Creator.
books.description: Chapters 1–11 cover the whole human race: creation, Adam and Eve's disobedience, Cain and Abel, the flood, and the tower of Babel. From chapter 12 the focus narrows to one man, Abraham, and God's promise to bless all nations through his seed. The promise passes through Isaac and Jacob to Jacob's twelve sons, and the book ends with Joseph saving his family in Egypt: 'ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.'

key_verses.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.

books.christ: The promised seed of the woman who will crush the serpent (3:15), and the seed of Abraham in whom all nations are blessed (Galatians 3:16).

books.name: Exodus
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Shemot, 'Names'. The Greek Exodos means 'going out'.
books.summary: God rescues Israel from slavery in Egypt, gives the Law at Sinai, and comes to live among them in the tabernacle.
books.author: Moses (traditional)
books.author_note: Jewish and Christian tradition, and Jesus himself ('the law of Moses', Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Moses is recorded writing parts of it (Exodus 24:4; Deuteronomy 31:9). Many modern scholars see it as compiled from several sources over centuries and completed around the exile; conservative scholars hold to Mosaic authorship with later editorial touches such as the account of Moses' death.
books.date: c. 1446–1406 BC by the traditional dating
books.audience: The Israelites delivered from Egypt
books.setting: Egypt and Sinai; from Joseph's death to the tabernacle set up in the second year after the Exodus (mid-15th or 13th century BC)
books.origin: Exodus is Israel's founding story. Moses is recorded writing down 'all the words of the LORD' (24:4), and the book preserves the covenant, the Ten Commandments and detailed plans for Israel's worship. Its events — Passover, the Red Sea, Sinai — became the pattern for every later act of salvation in the Bible.
books.description: A new Pharaoh enslaves Israel. God calls Moses at the burning bush, reveals his name, I AM THAT I AM, and sends ten plagues on Egypt. At the first Passover the blood of a lamb protects Israel's firstborn, and God parts the Red Sea. At Mount Sinai he gives the Ten Commandments and makes a covenant. Even after the golden calf, God renews the covenant, and the book ends with his glory filling the finished tabernacle.

outline.title: Slavery and the call of Moses
The golden calf and the covenant renewed

key_verses.text: And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.

And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt.
I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
Then a cloud covered the tent of the congregation, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.

books.christ: Christ is 'our passover… sacrificed for us' (1 Corinthians 5:7), the Word who 'dwelt' (tabernacled) among us (John 1:14), and the one who said 'Before Abraham was, I am' (John 8:58).

books.name: Leviticus
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Vayikra, 'And he called'. The Greek Leuitikon means 'about the Levites'.
books.summary: How a sinful people can live with a holy God: sacrifices, priests, purity, the Day of Atonement and the call to be holy.
books.author: Moses (traditional)
books.author_note: Jewish and Christian tradition, and Jesus himself ('the law of Moses', Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Moses is recorded writing parts of it (Exodus 24:4; Deuteronomy 31:9). Many modern scholars see it as compiled from several sources over centuries and completed around the exile; conservative scholars hold to Mosaic authorship with later editorial touches such as the account of Moses' death.
books.date: c. 1446–1406 BC by the traditional dating
books.audience: Israel's priests and people at Sinai
books.setting: At Mount Sinai, in about the month after the tabernacle was set up
books.origin: Leviticus is mostly speech: over thirty times it says 'the LORD spake unto Moses'. It was the handbook for the tabernacle and the priesthood of Aaron's family, and for how ordinary Israelites were to worship and live. Jewish children traditionally began their study of Scripture here.
books.description: It opens with five kinds of offering, then the ordination of Aaron and his sons, when Nadab and Abihu die for offering 'strange fire'. Laws on clean and unclean food, childbirth and skin disease follow. At the centre (chapter 16) is the Day of Atonement, with the scapegoat. The 'Holiness Code' (17–26) covers everyday life, the feasts, the sabbath year and the jubilee, including 'thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself'.

key_verses.text: For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.
Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.

books.christ: Hebrews presents Jesus as the great high priest who entered the holy place 'by his own blood', once for all (Hebrews 9:11-12).

books.name: Numbers
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Bemidbar, 'In the wilderness'. The Greek Arithmoi, 'Numbers', comes from its two censuses.
books.summary: Forty years in the wilderness: Israel's unbelief at the edge of the promised land, and God's faithfulness to a new generation.
books.author: Moses (traditional)
books.author_note: Jewish and Christian tradition, and Jesus himself ('the law of Moses', Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Moses is recorded writing parts of it (Exodus 24:4; Deuteronomy 31:9). Many modern scholars see it as compiled from several sources over centuries and completed around the exile; conservative scholars hold to Mosaic authorship with later editorial touches such as the account of Moses' death. Numbers 33:2 says Moses recorded the journey's stages.
books.date: c. 1406 BC by the traditional dating
books.audience: The new generation about to enter Canaan
books.setting: From Sinai to the plains of Moab; about 38 years of wandering
books.origin: Numbers records the journey between Sinai and the Jordan, with two censuses of fighting men (chapters 1 and 26) that bracket the death of one generation and the rise of the next. Its stories became warnings for later believers (1 Corinthians 10:1-11; Hebrews 3–4).
books.description: Israel sets out from Sinai in order, with the ark leading. Complaints follow, then the decisive failure: ten spies frighten the people out of entering Canaan, and God sentences them to forty years in the wilderness. Korah rebels, Moses strikes the rock and is barred from the land, and bitten Israelites are healed by looking at a bronze serpent. On the plains of Moab the prophet Balaam, hired to curse Israel, can only bless it. A new census and preparations for the land close the book.

key_verses.text: The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.
Only rebel not ye against the LORD, neither fear ye the people of the land; for they are bread for us: their defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us: fear them not.
And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.
God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?

books.christ: 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up' (John 3:14). Balaam foresees 'a Star out of Jacob' (24:17).

books.name: Deuteronomy
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Devarim, 'Words'. The Greek Deuteronomion, 'second law', comes from 17:18.
books.summary: Moses' farewell sermons on the plains of Moab, restating the Law and calling Israel to love God and choose life.
books.author: Moses (traditional); the account of his death (ch. 34) was added by another hand
books.author_note: Jewish and Christian tradition, and Jesus himself ('the law of Moses', Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Moses is recorded writing parts of it (Exodus 24:4; Deuteronomy 31:9). Many modern scholars see it as compiled from several sources over centuries and completed around the exile; conservative scholars hold to Mosaic authorship with later editorial touches such as the account of Moses' death. Many scholars link Deuteronomy with the 'book of the law' found in the Temple under King Josiah (2 Kings 22), c. 622 BC.
books.date: c. 1406 BC by the traditional dating
books.audience: The generation about to enter Canaan
books.setting: The plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, in the last month of Moses' life
books.origin: Deuteronomy is framed as three speeches Moses gave before his death, followed by his song and blessing. Its structure resembles ancient treaties: history, stipulations, blessings and curses, witnesses. It is quoted over 80 times in the New Testament, and Jesus answered all three of Satan's temptations from it.
books.description: Moses reviews the journey from Horeb, then restates the Ten Commandments and the Shema: 'Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart.' Laws for worship, justice, kings, prophets and everyday life follow, then the blessings of obedience and the curses of rebellion. Joshua is commissioned, and Moses views the land from Mount Nebo and dies.

outline.title: Joshua, Moses' song and blessing, Moses' death

key_verses.text: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.

And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live.
I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live:
Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.

books.christ: The prophet 'like unto me' whom God would raise up (18:15), fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 3:22-26).

groups.name: History Books
groups.description: Basically, Israel's history — from entering Canaan under Joshua, through the judges and the kings, the division and fall of the kingdom, to the exile in Babylon and the return to rebuild Jerusalem.

key_chapters.note: Nehemiah goes to rebuild the walls

books.name: Joshua
books.name_meaning: Named after its hero; Joshua (Yehoshua) means 'the LORD is salvation' — the same name as Jesus.
books.summary: Israel crosses the Jordan, conquers Canaan under Joshua, and divides the land among the tribes.
books.author: Joshua (traditional), with later additions
books.author_note: The Talmud credits Joshua with the book, except the account of his death, added by Eleazar and Phinehas. Joshua is said to have written 'these words in the book of the law of God' (24:26). In the Hebrew Bible, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings are the 'Former Prophets'. Many scholars read them as one history, shaped by Deuteronomy's teaching and completed during the exile.
books.date: c. 1400–1370 BC by the traditional dating; final form debated
books.audience: Israel settled in the land
books.setting: Canaan, from the crossing of the Jordan to Joshua's death (about 25 years)
books.origin: Joshua continues directly from Deuteronomy: the same promise of land, now being kept. It includes eyewitness-style details ('unto this day', 4:9) alongside detailed boundary lists for each tribe, which served as Israel's land register.
books.description: God tells Joshua to be strong and courageous. Rahab hides the spies, the Jordan parts, and Jericho's walls fall at the shout of the people. Achan's hidden sin causes defeat at Ai. The Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty, and the sun stands still while Joshua defeats the southern kings. After the northern campaign the land is divided by lot, cities of refuge are set up, and Joshua's farewell ends with 'as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.'

outline.title: Joshua's farewell and the covenant renewed

key_verses.text: Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.

So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city.
There failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

books.christ: Joshua bears the name Jesus bears; he leads God's people into rest, a picture Hebrews 4 fulfils in Christ. Rahab of Jericho is in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:5).

books.name: Judges
books.name_meaning: Named after the 'judges' (shophetim) — deliverers God raised up to rescue Israel.
books.summary: A downward spiral of sin, oppression and rescue, through Deborah, Gideon and Samson, when 'every man did that which was right in his own eyes'.
books.author: Unknown (Jewish tradition: Samuel)
books.author_note: The book does not name its author. The repeated line 'In those days there was no king in Israel' suggests it was written early in the monarchy. In the Hebrew Bible, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings are the 'Former Prophets'. Many scholars read them as one history, shaped by Deuteronomy's teaching and completed during the exile.
books.date: Probably early monarchy, c. 1050–1000 BC; final form debated
books.audience: Israel under its first kings
books.setting: From Joshua's death to the time of Samuel (c. 1375–1050 BC traditionally)
books.origin: Judges gathers the stories of twelve deliverers from different tribes and arranges them in a repeating cycle: Israel sins, God gives them to an enemy, they cry out, God raises a judge, the land has rest, then the cycle starts again, each time worse.
books.description: Othniel, left-handed Ehud and Shamgar come first. Deborah and Barak defeat Sisera, whom Jael kills with a tent peg. Gideon routs Midian with three hundred men, trumpets and torches. Jephthah makes a tragic vow. Samson, the strongest judge, is the weakest in character and dies pulling down Dagon's temple. The last chapters show the nation's collapse: a private idol, a tribe stealing it, a Levite's concubine murdered, and civil war against Benjamin.

outline.title: The judges, from Othniel to Samson

key_verses.text: Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them.
And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.
In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.

books.christ: Each judge is a flawed, temporary saviour; the book leaves Israel longing for a true King and Deliverer.

books.name: Ruth
books.name_meaning: Named after Ruth the Moabitess; the name may mean 'friend' or 'companion'.
books.summary: In the dark days of the judges, a loyal Moabite widow finds refuge under the wings of Israel's God and becomes the great-grandmother of David.
books.author: Unknown (Jewish tradition: Samuel)
books.author_note: The book does not name its author. It ends with David's genealogy, so it was written in or after David's time. In the Hebrew Bible it sits among the 'Writings' and is read at the feast of Weeks (Pentecost).
books.date: During or after David's reign (c. 1000 BC or later)
books.audience: Israel under the monarchy
books.setting: Bethlehem and Moab, 'in the days when the judges ruled'
books.origin: A short, carefully crafted story set at harvest time. Its genealogy ties an ordinary family's faithfulness to the royal line, showing that God was at work even in the chaos of the judges.
books.description: Famine drives Elimelech and Naomi to Moab, where Naomi's husband and sons die. Naomi returns to Bethlehem, and her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her: 'whither thou goest, I will go.' Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz, a relative, who treats her kindly. At Naomi's urging Ruth asks Boaz to act as kinsman-redeemer; he marries her, and their son Obed becomes the grandfather of David.

outline.title: Naomi and Ruth return to Bethlehem
Boaz redeems; the line of David

key_verses.text: And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.
And the women her neighbours gave it a name, saying, There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David.

books.christ: Boaz the kinsman-redeemer pictures Christ who redeems at his own cost; Ruth is named in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:5).

books.name: 1 Samuel
books.name_meaning: Named after Samuel, the last judge and the prophet who anointed Israel's first two kings. Samuel means 'heard of God' or 'name of God'.
books.summary: Israel moves from judges to kings: Samuel's birth and ministry, Saul's rise and rejection, and young David's rise.
books.author: Unknown (tradition: Samuel, Nathan and Gad)
books.author_note: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition (Talmud, Bava Batra 14b–15a) says Samuel wrote the early part and the prophets Nathan and Gad completed it, drawing on 1 Chronicles 29:29. 1 and 2 Samuel were one book in Hebrew; the Greek translators split it into two. In the Hebrew Bible, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings are the 'Former Prophets'. Many scholars read them as one history, shaped by Deuteronomy's teaching and completed during the exile.
books.date: After Solomon's death (it mentions 'the kings of Judah', 27:6), c. 930 BC or later
books.audience: Israel and Judah under the kings
books.setting: c. 1105–1010 BC; Shiloh, Ramah, Gibeah and the wilderness of Judah
books.origin: Samuel was written from prophetic records of the transition to monarchy. It is frank about its heroes' failures and shows that God, not human strength, raises and brings down kings.
books.description: Barren Hannah prays for a son and gives Samuel to God's service. The ark is captured by the Philistines and returned. The people demand a king 'like all the nations', and God gives them Saul, who begins well but disobeys and is rejected: 'to obey is better than sacrifice'. Samuel anoints the shepherd boy David, who kills Goliath, becomes Jonathan's friend, and flees Saul's jealousy for years, twice sparing Saul's life. The book ends with Saul's death on Mount Gilboa.

key_verses.text: And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.
And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.

Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.

books.christ: Hannah's song first speaks of the LORD's 'anointed' (Messiah, 2:10); David, the anointed shepherd-king from Bethlehem, foreshadows Christ.

books.name: 2 Samuel
books.name_meaning: The second half of the book of Samuel.
books.summary: David's reign: his triumphs, God's covenant with his house, his sin with Bathsheba, and the troubles that followed.
books.author: Unknown (tradition: Nathan and Gad)
books.author_note: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition (Talmud, Bava Batra 14b–15a) says Samuel wrote the early part and the prophets Nathan and Gad completed it, drawing on 1 Chronicles 29:29. 1 and 2 Samuel were one book in Hebrew; the Greek translators split it into two. In the Hebrew Bible, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings are the 'Former Prophets'. Many scholars read them as one history, shaped by Deuteronomy's teaching and completed during the exile.
books.date: After Solomon's death, c. 930 BC or later
books.audience: Israel and Judah under the kings
books.setting: c. 1010–970 BC; Hebron and Jerusalem
books.origin: The book is built around the covenant God made with David in chapter 7 and then shows, without hiding anything, how David's own sin brought 'the sword' into his house.
books.description: David mourns Saul and Jonathan, is made king over Judah and then all Israel, takes Jerusalem, and brings up the ark with dancing. God promises him an everlasting house and throne. At the height of his power David takes Bathsheba and has Uriah killed; Nathan confronts him — 'Thou art the man' — and David repents. Amnon's crime, Absalom's revolt and death, and further rebellions follow. The book closes with David's songs, his mighty men and the census plague.

key_verses.text: And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever.
And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul;
And he said, The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer;

books.christ: The promise of an eternal throne for David's son (7:12-16) is fulfilled in Jesus, 'the son of David' (Luke 1:32-33).

books.name: 1 Kings
books.name_meaning: Named after the kings of Israel and Judah whose reigns it records.
books.summary: Solomon's glory and the Temple, the kingdom's split into Israel and Judah, and Elijah's stand against Baal.
books.author: Unknown (Jewish tradition: Jeremiah)
books.author_note: The author is not named; Jewish tradition credits Jeremiah. The writer cites sources such as 'the book of the acts of Solomon' and the chronicles of the kings of Israel and Judah. 1 and 2 Kings were one book in Hebrew. In the Hebrew Bible, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings are the 'Former Prophets'. Many scholars read them as one history, shaped by Deuteronomy's teaching and completed during the exile.
books.date: Completed after 561 BC (2 Kings 25:27), during the exile
books.audience: Exiles asking why the kingdom fell
books.setting: c. 970–853 BC; Jerusalem and Samaria
books.origin: Kings judges every ruler by one measure — faithfulness to the LORD — and explains the exile as the result of centuries of idolatry, while holding on to God's promise to David.
books.description: Solomon succeeds David, asks God for wisdom, builds and dedicates the Temple, and receives the queen of Sheba. But his foreign wives turn his heart to other gods. Under his son Rehoboam the ten northern tribes break away under Jeroboam, who sets up golden calves. A succession of northern kings follows, down to Ahab and Jezebel, who promote Baal. Elijah announces a drought, defeats the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, hears God's 'still small voice', and confronts Ahab over Naboth's vineyard.

key_verses.text: Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people?
But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?

So when all Israel saw that the king hearkened not unto them, the people answered the king, saying, What portion have we in David? neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: to your tents, O Israel: now see to thine own house, David. So Israel departed unto their tents.
And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.

books.christ: Jesus is 'greater than Solomon' (Matthew 12:42) and the true Temple (John 2:19-21).

books.name: 2 Kings
books.name_meaning: The second half of the book of Kings.
books.summary: Elisha's miracles, the fall of Israel to Assyria, the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah, and Jerusalem's fall to Babylon.
books.author: Unknown (Jewish tradition: Jeremiah)
books.author_note: The author is not named; Jewish tradition credits Jeremiah. The writer cites sources such as 'the book of the acts of Solomon' and the chronicles of the kings of Israel and Judah. 1 and 2 Kings were one book in Hebrew. In the Hebrew Bible, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings are the 'Former Prophets'. Many scholars read them as one history, shaped by Deuteronomy's teaching and completed during the exile.
books.date: Completed after 561 BC, during the exile
books.audience: Exiles in Babylon
books.setting: c. 853–561 BC; Israel, Judah, Assyria and Babylon
books.origin: The second half of Kings follows both kingdoms to their end. Its final paragraph — King Jehoiachin released from prison and fed at the king's table — leaves a thread of hope for David's line.
books.description: Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind, and Elisha receives a double portion of his spirit, raising a dead boy and healing Naaman. Jehu wipes out Ahab's house. The northern kingdom falls to Assyria in 722 BC, and chapter 17 explains why. In Judah, Hezekiah trusts God and Jerusalem is delivered from Sennacherib; Josiah finds the book of the law and leads a great reform. But Manasseh's evil sealed Judah's fate, and Nebuchadnezzar burns Jerusalem and the Temple in 586 BC.

outline.title: Israel and Judah to the fall of Samaria
Judah alone, to the fall of Jerusalem

key_verses.text: And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.

Yet the LORD testified against Israel, and against Judah, by all the prophets, and by all the seers, saying, Turn ye from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.

And like unto him was there no king before him, that turned to the LORD with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might, according to all the law of Moses; neither after him arose there any like him.

books.christ: Elisha's ministry of healing, raising the dead and feeding many with little foreshadows Jesus' miracles (Luke 4:27).

books.name: 1 Chronicles
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Divre ha-Yamim, 'the words (events) of the days'. The Greek Paraleipomena means 'things left out'; 'Chronicles' comes from Jerome.
books.summary: Israel's story retold for the returned exiles: genealogies from Adam, then David's reign and his preparations for the Temple.
books.author: The Chronicler (Jewish tradition: Ezra)
books.author_note: The author, often called 'the Chronicler', is not named; Jewish tradition credits Ezra, and the last verses of 2 Chronicles repeat the opening of Ezra. The writer drew on Samuel and Kings and on many named records. 1 and 2 Chronicles were one book in Hebrew, the last book of the Hebrew Bible.
books.audience: Jews who had returned from exile
books.setting: From Adam to David's death (c. 970 BC)
books.origin: Written after the exile, Chronicles retells history from a priestly angle to remind a small, struggling community that they were still the people of God's covenant with David, centred on the Temple and true worship.
books.description: Nine chapters of genealogy run from Adam through the tribes, including the short prayer of Jabez. Saul's death is told briefly, then David's reign in detail: bringing the ark to Jerusalem with music and praise, God's covenant, his victories, and especially his careful preparations for the Temple — materials, Levites, singers and gatekeepers. David's sin with Bathsheba is not retold.

outline.title: Genealogies from Adam to the returned exiles
David made king; the ark comes to Jerusalem
Preparing for the Temple; Solomon crowned

key_verses.text: And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested.
O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever.

Thine, O LORD, is the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty: for all that is in the heaven and in the earth is thine; thine is the kingdom, O LORD, and thou art exalted as head above all.

books.christ: The genealogies preserve the line of David from which the Messiah would come (Matthew 1:1).

books.name: 2 Chronicles
books.name_meaning: The second half of Chronicles.
books.summary: The kings of Judah from Solomon's Temple to the exile, ending with Cyrus' decree to rebuild.
books.author: The Chronicler (Jewish tradition: Ezra)
books.author_note: The author, often called 'the Chronicler', is not named; Jewish tradition credits Ezra, and the last verses of 2 Chronicles repeat the opening of Ezra. The writer drew on Samuel and Kings and on many named records. 1 and 2 Chronicles were one book in Hebrew, the last book of the Hebrew Bible.
books.audience: Jews who had returned from exile
books.setting: c. 970–538 BC; Jerusalem
books.origin: The second half of Chronicles focuses on Judah and its Temple, highlighting the kings who sought God and the revivals they led, and ending on the hopeful note of return.
books.description: Solomon builds and dedicates the Temple, and God answers: 'If my people… shall humble themselves, and pray… then will I hear from heaven.' The northern kingdom is mostly left out. Judah's kings are judged by whether they sought the LORD: Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah lead revivals, and even wicked Manasseh repents in exile. The book ends with Jerusalem's fall and the decree of Cyrus.

outline.title: Hezekiah, Josiah, the exile and Cyrus

key_verses.text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.

For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars.

And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the LORD unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s.

Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, All the kingdoms of the earth hath the LORD God of heaven given me; and he hath charged me to build him an house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is there among you of all his people? The LORD his God be with him, and let him go up.

books.christ: The Temple where God put his name points to Christ, in whom 'dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily' (Colossians 2:9).

books.name: Ezra
books.name_meaning: Named after Ezra the priest and scribe; Ezra means 'help'.
books.summary: The exiles return from Babylon under Cyrus, rebuild the Temple, and are renewed in God's Law under Ezra.
books.author: Ezra (traditional)
books.author_note: Jewish tradition names Ezra as author; chapters 7–9 are written in the first person. Ezra and Nehemiah were one book in the Hebrew Bible. Parts (4:8–6:18; 7:12-26) are in Aramaic, the official language of the Persian empire, and quote royal letters.
books.audience: The returned community in Judah
books.setting: 538–c. 457 BC; Babylon and Jerusalem under Persian rule
books.origin: Ezra draws on official documents — Cyrus' decree, lists of returning families, letters to and from Persian kings — to show God keeping his word through Jeremiah that the exile would end.
books.description: Cyrus lets the Jews go home, and about 50,000 return under Zerubbabel. They rebuild the altar and lay the Temple's foundation, but local opposition stops the work for years. Encouraged by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, they finish the Temple in 516 BC. Decades later Ezra, 'a ready scribe in the law of Moses', arrives from Babylon and leads the people to repent of marrying into pagan peoples.

outline.title: The return and the Temple rebuilt

key_verses.text: Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD God of Israel, (he is the God,) which is in Jerusalem.

And they sang together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the LORD; because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel. And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.
For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.

books.christ: God preserves his people and the line of David (Zerubbabel appears in Jesus' genealogy, Matthew 1:12) for the coming of Christ.

books.name: Nehemiah
books.name_meaning: Named after Nehemiah, the Persian king's cupbearer; Nehemiah means 'the LORD comforts'.
books.summary: Nehemiah leaves the Persian court to rebuild Jerusalem's walls in 52 days, and leads the people back to God's Law.
books.author: Nehemiah (his memoirs), with Ezra
books.author_note: Much of the book is Nehemiah's own first-person memoir ('the words of Nehemiah', 1:1). It was one book with Ezra in the Hebrew Bible.
books.audience: The returned community in Judah
books.setting: 445–c. 432 BC; Susa and Jerusalem
books.origin: Nehemiah's memoir, full of short prayers ('Remember me, O my God'), is combined with lists and records of the community's covenant renewal. Outside records, the Elephantine papyri, name his opponent Sanballat as governor of Samaria.
books.description: Hearing that Jerusalem's walls lie in ruins, Nehemiah weeps, prays and asks King Artaxerxes for leave to rebuild them. Despite mockery and threats from Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem, the people build with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, and finish in 52 days. Ezra reads the Law to the people, who weep, then celebrate: 'the joy of the LORD is your strength.' They confess their sins and sign a covenant, and Nehemiah later returns to correct abuses.

outline.title: The Law read and the covenant renewed

key_verses.text: O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name: and prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. For I was the king’s cupbearer.
So the wall was finished in the twenty and fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty and two days.

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.

books.christ: Nehemiah leaves a royal palace to restore a ruined city and its people — a picture of the one who 'became poor' to restore us (2 Corinthians 8:9).

books.name: Esther
books.name_meaning: Named after Queen Esther; her Persian name probably means 'star'. Her Hebrew name was Hadassah, 'myrtle'.
books.summary: A Jewish orphan becomes queen of Persia and risks her life to save her people from Haman's plot — the origin of Purim.
books.author: Unknown
books.author_note: The author is not named; suggestions include Mordecai (9:20 says he 'wrote these things') or a later Persian-era Jew. The book never mentions God by name, yet his providence runs through every turn of the story.
books.audience: Jews of the Persian empire
books.setting: Shushan (Susa), 483–473 BC, in the reign of Ahasuerus (Xerxes I)
books.origin: Esther explains the origin of the feast of Purim ('lots'), still read aloud each year in synagogues. Its details of the Persian court match what is known from Greek historians and the palace excavated at Susa.
books.description: King Ahasuerus deposes Queen Vashti and chooses Esther, who hides that she is Jewish. Her cousin Mordecai refuses to bow to Haman, the king's favourite, so Haman plots to destroy all the Jews. Mordecai urges Esther: 'who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' She fasts and goes to the king uninvited, saying 'if I perish, I perish.' Haman is hanged on his own gallows, and the Jews are allowed to defend themselves.

outline.title: Deliverance and the feast of Purim

key_verses.text: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?

Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.

books.christ: Esther risks death to intercede for her condemned people before the king — a shadow of Christ, who 'ever liveth to make intercession' (Hebrews 7:25).

groups.name: Poetry and Wisdom
groups.description: The songs, prayers and wisdom of Israel: how to worship, how to suffer, how to live wisely, and how to love. Written mostly in Hebrew poetry, which rhymes ideas rather than sounds — each line echoes or answers the one before.

books.name: Job
books.name_meaning: Named after Job, a righteous man of the land of Uz. The name may mean 'where is the father?' or 'persecuted one'.
books.summary: A blameless man loses everything, argues with his friends about why, and finally meets God in the whirlwind.
books.author: Unknown (Jewish tradition: Moses)
books.author_note: The author is not named. The Talmud credits Moses; others suggest Job himself, Solomon or a later wise man. Job's world — wealth in flocks, the father offering sacrifices for his family, a lifespan of 140 years after his trials — fits the age of the patriarchs.
books.date: Unknown; the setting is patriarchal, and the date of writing is widely debated
books.audience: The wise and the suffering of every age
books.setting: The land of Uz (probably east or south-east of Canaan, near Edom), in the patriarchal era
books.origin: Job is framed by a prose prologue and epilogue around long poetic speeches, some of the finest and hardest Hebrew poetry in the Bible. Ezekiel names Job with Noah and Daniel as a model of righteousness (Ezekiel 14:14), and James praises his patience (James 5:11).
books.description: Satan claims Job serves God only for what he gets. God allows him to be tested: Job loses his children, wealth and health, yet says 'the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.' Three friends insist he must be suffering for his sin; Job protests his innocence and longs to argue his case with God. Young Elihu speaks next. Then God answers from the whirlwind — not with explanations, but with the wonders of creation — and Job bows. God rebukes the friends and restores Job twice over.

key_verses.text: And said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.

books.christ: Job longs for a 'daysman' to stand between God and man (9:33) and declares 'I know that my redeemer liveth' (19:25) — fulfilled in the one mediator, Christ (1 Timothy 2:5).

books.name: Psalms
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Tehillim, 'Praises'. The Greek psalmoi means songs sung to a stringed instrument.
books.summary: Israel's hymn book: 150 prayers and songs of praise, lament, thanksgiving, trust and hope in the coming King.
books.author: Many authors, chiefly David
books.author_note: The headings credit 73 psalms to David, 12 to Asaph, 11 to the sons of Korah, 2 to Solomon, 1 each to Moses (Psalm 90), Heman and Ethan; about 50 have no named author. The collection grew over some 900 years and was arranged in its final form after the exile.
books.date: c. 1400 BC (Psalm 90) to after the exile (Psalm 137); final collection c. 5th–4th century BC
books.audience: Israel at worship, and every believer at prayer
books.setting: From Moses in the wilderness through David's reign to the exile and return
books.origin: The psalms were sung in the Temple, many with instructions for the chief musician. They are gathered into five books, each ending with a doxology, perhaps echoing the five books of Moses. Psalms is the Old Testament book most quoted in the New.
books.description: Every human emotion is here, brought before God: joy and grief, confidence and doubt, anger and repentance. There are hymns of praise, laments, songs of thanks, royal psalms about the king, wisdom psalms like Psalm 1, and the long Psalm 119, an acrostic on the Word of God. Well-loved psalms include 23 ('The LORD is my shepherd'), 51 (David's repentance), 91 and 103. The book ends in a crescendo of 'Praise ye the LORD'.

key_verses.text: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.  But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.

books.christ: Jesus said the psalms were written 'concerning me' (Luke 24:44). Psalm 2 (the Son), 22 (the cross), 16 (the resurrection) and 110 (the priest-king) are all applied to him in the New Testament.

books.name: Proverbs
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Mishlei, 'Proverbs of', from the book's first words: 'The proverbs of Solomon'.
books.summary: Short, practical sayings on how to live wisely before God — at work, at home, in speech and with money.
books.author: Mainly Solomon, with Agur and King Lemuel
books.author_note: Solomon 'spake three thousand proverbs' (1 Kings 4:32). The book names several collections: Solomon's (1:1; 10:1), 'the words of the wise' (22:17), Solomon's proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men (25:1), Agur (30) and Lemuel (31).
books.date: Mainly 10th century BC; compiled by c. 700 BC (Hezekiah) and finished later
books.audience: Young people and all who would be wise
books.setting: Everyday life in Israel under the kings
books.origin: Proverbs belongs to a wider tradition of wisdom writing in the ancient Near East; one section (22:17–24:22) closely resembles the Egyptian 'Instruction of Amenemope'. What sets it apart is its foundation: 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.'
books.description: The first nine chapters are a father's appeals to his son to choose Wisdom — pictured as a noble woman calling in the streets — over folly and the adulteress. The rest are mostly two-line sayings on diligence and laziness, honesty, anger, friendship, pride, words, wealth, justice and family. The book ends with a poem in praise of the virtuous woman.

outline.title: Solomon's proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men
Agur, Lemuel and the virtuous woman

key_verses.text: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.

books.christ: Christ is 'made unto us wisdom' (1 Corinthians 1:30), and in him 'are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge' (Colossians 2:3); many see him prefigured in Wisdom of Proverbs 8.

books.name: Ecclesiastes
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Qoheleth, 'the Preacher' or 'one who gathers an assembly'. Ecclesiastes is the Greek form.
books.summary: The Preacher searches for meaning 'under the sun' and finds everything vanity — except fearing God and keeping his commandments.
books.author: 'The Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem' — traditionally Solomon
books.author_note: Jewish and Christian tradition identify the Preacher with Solomon, whose wisdom and wealth fit the book. Many scholars date the language to after the exile and see the author writing in Solomon's voice.
books.date: c. 935 BC (Solomon, traditional) or 5th–3rd century BC
books.audience: Anyone asking what life is for
books.setting: Jerusalem; reflections of an old, wise king
books.origin: Ecclesiastes is a wisdom book that tests conventional answers against hard reality — death, injustice, chance. It is read in synagogues at the feast of Tabernacles.
books.description: 'Vanity of vanities; all is vanity' — the Preacher's word (hebel) means breath or vapour. He tries pleasure, work, wealth and wisdom and finds none of them lasting. Yet he also commends enjoying food, work and marriage as gifts from God: 'To every thing there is a season.' He ends by urging the young to 'Remember now thy Creator' and concludes: 'Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.'

outline.title: All is vanity: the Preacher's search

key_verses.text: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.

books.christ: Life 'under the sun' is vanity; Christ brings 'life and immortality to light' (2 Timothy 1:10), so that labour in the Lord is 'not in vain' (1 Corinthians 15:58).

books.name: Song of Solomon
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Shir ha-Shirim, 'The Song of Songs' — the finest of songs. Also called Canticles.
books.summary: A love poem between a bride and her beloved, celebrating the beauty and strength of married love.
books.author: Solomon (1:1)
books.author_note: The opening line ascribes the song to Solomon, who wrote 1,005 songs (1 Kings 4:32). Some read the heading as 'for' or 'about' Solomon and date the poem later.
books.audience: Israel; read in synagogues at Passover
books.setting: The countryside and royal court of Israel
books.origin: The Song is a collection of love poetry in dialogue — the bride, the beloved and a chorus of 'daughters of Jerusalem'. Jewish tradition has long read it also as a picture of God's love for Israel; Christian tradition, of Christ's love for the Church.
books.description: The lovers long for each other, praise each other's beauty in rich imagery of gardens, vineyards and spices, and are married. The bride fears losing her beloved and searches the city for him. The song closes with one of the Bible's great statements about love: 'love is strong as death… Many waters cannot quench love.' It repeatedly warns: 'stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.'

key_verses.text: He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.

Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame. Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.

books.christ: The New Testament pictures Christ as the Bridegroom and the Church as his bride (Ephesians 5:25-32; Revelation 19:7).

groups.name: Major Prophets
groups.description: Called 'major' for their length, not their importance. Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel warned Judah before and during its fall to Babylon; Lamentations mourns Jerusalem; Daniel was faithful in exile. Together they promise a new covenant and a coming King.

books.name: Isaiah
books.name_meaning: Named after Isaiah son of Amoz; Isaiah (Yeshayahu) means 'the LORD is salvation'.
books.summary: Judgement and comfort for Jerusalem, and the Bible's clearest Old Testament portraits of the coming Messiah and suffering Servant.
books.author: Isaiah son of Amoz
books.author_note: Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1). Many scholars assign chapters 40–66 to later prophets writing during and after the exile ('Second' and 'Third Isaiah'), partly because they name Cyrus. The traditional view holds one author; the New Testament quotes both halves as Isaiah's (John 12:38-41). The complete Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran dates to about 125 BC.
books.audience: Judah and Jerusalem; later, the exiles
books.setting: Jerusalem during the Assyrian crisis, looking ahead to Babylon and the return
books.origin: Isaiah received his call in a vision of the LORD 'high and lifted up' in the Temple in the year King Uzziah died (c. 740 BC). He advised kings through the Syro-Ephraimite war and Sennacherib's siege. Jewish tradition says he was martyred under Manasseh.
books.description: Chapters 1–39 condemn Judah's sin and the pride of the nations, but promise a child called Immanuel and a son whose name is 'Wonderful, Counseller, The mighty God'. A historical section tells of Jerusalem's deliverance from Assyria. Chapters 40–66 open with 'Comfort ye my people', announce return from exile, describe the Servant of the LORD who is 'wounded for our transgressions', and end with new heavens and a new earth.

outline.title: Judgement and hope for Judah; Immanuel
The LORD's worldwide judgement and salvation
Comfort for the exiles; the Servant
Glory for Zion; new heavens and new earth

key_verses.text: Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.

books.christ: Isaiah is called the 'fifth gospel': the virgin birth (7:14), the divine child (9:6), the Spirit-anointed preacher (61:1, read by Jesus in Luke 4:18), and the Servant who bears our sins (53).

books.name: Jeremiah
books.name_meaning: Named after Jeremiah son of Hilkiah; the name probably means 'the LORD exalts' or 'the LORD throws down'.
books.summary: The 'weeping prophet' warns Judah for forty years before Babylon destroys Jerusalem, and promises a new covenant.
books.author: Jeremiah, with his scribe Baruch
books.author_note: Jeremiah, a priest from Anathoth, dictated his prophecies to Baruch son of Neriah; when King Jehoiakim burned the scroll, they wrote it again (chapter 36). The Greek Septuagint version is about an eighth shorter and orders the chapters differently, and both forms are found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
books.audience: Judah before and after the fall of Jerusalem
books.setting: Jerusalem, from Josiah's 13th year to after 586 BC; ends in Egypt
books.origin: Jeremiah's book mixes sermons, symbolic actions, personal laments ('confessions') and biography. It is the longest book of the Bible by word count. Seal impressions bearing the names of 'Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe' (Baruch) and other officials named in the book have been found.
books.description: Called as a youth — 'Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee' — Jeremiah condemns Judah's idolatry and false prophets' cries of 'peace, peace'. He is beaten, imprisoned and thrown into a muddy cistern for urging surrender to Babylon. Yet he buys a field as a sign of future return, tells the exiles to seek the peace of Babylon for seventy years, and promises a new covenant written on the heart. He witnesses Jerusalem's fall and is taken to Egypt.

outline.title: Jeremiah's sufferings and the fall of Jerusalem; the new covenant

key_verses.text: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.

books.christ: The new covenant (31:31-34) is established in Christ's blood (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:8-12). Jesus is the 'righteous Branch' raised unto David (23:5).

books.name: Lamentations
books.name_meaning: Hebrew Eikhah, 'How!' — the cry that opens the book. The Greek Threnoi means 'laments'.
books.summary: Five poems of grief over Jerusalem's destruction, with a shining word of hope at the centre: 'his compassions fail not'.
books.author: Unknown (tradition: Jeremiah)
books.author_note: The book is anonymous. The Septuagint and Jewish tradition credit Jeremiah, who is said to have written laments (2 Chronicles 35:25) and who witnessed the city's fall.
books.audience: The survivors of Jerusalem's fall
books.setting: Ruined Jerusalem after the Babylonian conquest
books.origin: Four of the five poems are acrostics following the Hebrew alphabet; chapter 3 gives three verses to each letter, making 66. The careful form gives shape to overwhelming grief. Lamentations is read in synagogues on Tisha B'Av, the day mourning the Temple's destruction.
books.description: Jerusalem is pictured as a widow weeping in the night with none to comfort her. The poems describe the siege, famine and destruction honestly, and admit that the city's sin brought it about. In the middle of the book the poet remembers: 'It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.' It ends with a prayer for renewal.

key_verses.text: It is of the LORD’S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old.

books.christ: Jesus wept over Jerusalem before its second destruction (Luke 19:41-44); he is the 'man of sorrows' who carries our griefs (Isaiah 53:3-4).

books.name: Ezekiel
books.name_meaning: Named after the priest Ezekiel son of Buzi; the name means 'God strengthens'.
books.summary: A priest in exile sees God's glory leave the Temple before Jerusalem falls, and return in a vision of a new temple and a revived people.
books.author: Ezekiel
books.author_note: Written largely in the first person, with dated prophecies spanning about 22 years (1:2; 29:17). Jewish tradition says the 'men of the Great Assembly' gave the book its final form.
books.audience: Jewish exiles in Babylon
books.setting: Tel-abib by the river Chebar in Babylonia, among the exiles deported in 597 BC
books.origin: Ezekiel was taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. Five years later he saw the living creatures and the throne of God by the river Chebar. His prophecies are precisely dated and often acted out in strange symbolic signs.
books.description: God makes Ezekiel a watchman for Israel. Before Jerusalem falls he acts out the siege and sees God's glory leave the Temple because of idolatry. He condemns the nations, including a famous lament over Tyre. After news of the city's fall he promises a new heart and a new spirit, a true shepherd from David's line, and in the valley of dry bones sees Israel raised to life. The book ends with a detailed vision of a new temple, a river of life, and a city named 'The LORD is there'.

outline.title: The vision of glory and Ezekiel's call
Restoration: new heart, true shepherd, dry bones

key_verses.text: Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
Thus saith the Lord GOD unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live:

books.christ: Jesus calls himself the good shepherd promised in Ezekiel 34 (John 10:11), and gives the living water of Ezekiel 47 (John 7:37-39).

books.name: Daniel
books.name_meaning: Named after Daniel, a young Jewish noble taken to Babylon; Daniel means 'God is my judge'.
books.summary: Faithfulness in a foreign empire — the fiery furnace and the lions' den — and visions of the kingdoms of the world giving way to God's kingdom.
books.author: Daniel (traditional)
books.author_note: Daniel speaks in the first person in chapters 7–12, and Jesus spoke of 'Daniel the prophet' (Matthew 24:15). Many scholars date the book's final form to c. 165 BC, reading chapter 11 as a description of Antiochus IV; the traditional view dates it to the 6th century BC. Chapters 2:4–7:28 are written in Aramaic. Fragments of Daniel were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
books.audience: God's people living under foreign empires
books.setting: Babylon and Persia, 605–c. 536 BC
books.origin: Daniel combines court stories about faithful Jews in the service of foreign kings with apocalyptic visions of the future. The Hebrew Bible places it among the Writings rather than the Prophets.
books.description: Daniel and his friends refuse the king's food and are blessed. Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar's dream of a statue of four metals broken by a stone 'cut out without hands'. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refuse to bow to the golden image and walk unharmed in the furnace with a fourth man. Belshazzar sees the writing on the wall, and Daniel is saved from the lions' den. In the visions four beasts rise from the sea, 'one like the Son of man' receives an everlasting kingdom, and Gabriel reveals the seventy weeks.
themes: God rules the kingdoms of men

outline.title: Stories of faithfulness in Babylon and Persia
Visions of the kingdoms and the end

key_verses.text: And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.

If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.

I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.

books.christ: Jesus' favourite title for himself, 'the Son of man', comes from Daniel 7:13-14, and he quoted it at his trial (Mark 14:62).

groups.name: Minor Prophets
groups.description: Twelve shorter prophetic books, kept on a single scroll in the Hebrew Bible and called 'The Twelve'. They span about 350 years, from Assyria's rise to the rebuilt Temple, calling Israel to justice, mercy and faithfulness.

books.name: Hosea
books.name_meaning: Named after Hosea son of Beeri; Hosea means 'salvation' — the same root as Joshua and Jesus.
books.summary: God tells Hosea to marry an unfaithful wife and win her back — a living picture of his love for unfaithful Israel.
books.author: Hosea son of Beeri
books.author_note: Hosea prophesied mainly to the northern kingdom in the last decades before its fall. In the Hebrew Bible the twelve minor prophets were copied together on one scroll, 'The Twelve'.
books.audience: The northern kingdom of Israel (often called Ephraim)
books.setting: Israel in its final, unstable years before Assyria destroyed Samaria
books.origin: Hosea's own broken marriage became his message. He is the only writing prophet from the northern kingdom, and his book is the first of the Twelve.
books.description: Hosea marries Gomer, who is unfaithful; their children receive names of judgement — 'Not my people', 'Not pitied'. Yet God tells Hosea to buy her back and love her again. The rest of the book pleads with Israel, whose love is 'as a morning cloud', and condemns its idolatry and alliances. God's heart breaks — 'How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?' — and the book ends with an invitation to return.

outline.title: Hosea's marriage: a picture of God and Israel
Call to return; promise of healing

key_verses.text: For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.

books.christ: 'Out of Egypt have I called my son' (11:1) is applied to Jesus (Matthew 2:15); Jesus twice quoted 'I desired mercy, and not sacrifice' (6:6; Matthew 9:13; 12:7).

books.name: Joel
books.name_meaning: Named after Joel son of Pethuel; Joel means 'the LORD is God'.
books.summary: A devastating locust plague becomes a warning of the Day of the LORD — and a promise that God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh.
books.author: Joel son of Pethuel
books.author_note: Nothing else is known of Joel, and the book gives no king's name, so its date is uncertain; proposals range from the 9th century BC to after the exile. In the Hebrew Bible the twelve minor prophets were copied together on one scroll, 'The Twelve'.
books.audience: Judah and Jerusalem
books.setting: Judah after a catastrophic locust invasion and drought
books.origin: Joel uses a real disaster to call the nation to repentance. Peter quoted Joel 2 on the day of Pentecost to explain the coming of the Holy Spirit.
books.description: Waves of locusts strip the land bare. Joel calls priests and people to fast and weep: 'rend your heart, and not your garments… for he is gracious and merciful.' God promises to 'restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten', then to pour out his Spirit on sons and daughters, old and young. The book ends with judgement on the nations in the valley of decision and blessing for Zion.

outline.title: The Day of the LORD; return, and the promise of the Spirit

key_verses.text: And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.
And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:

books.christ: Joel's promise of the Spirit was fulfilled at Pentecost after Jesus' ascension (Acts 2:16-21), and 'whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered' is applied to Christ (Romans 10:13).

books.name: Amos
books.name_meaning: Named after Amos; the name means 'burden' or 'burden-bearer'.
books.summary: A shepherd from Judah thunders against the luxury and injustice of prosperous Israel: 'let judgment run down as waters'.
books.author: Amos of Tekoa
books.author_note: Amos was 'among the herdmen of Tekoa' and 'a gatherer of sycomore fruit', not a professional prophet (7:14). He preached 'two years before the earthquake' in the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam II (1:1). In the Hebrew Bible the twelve minor prophets were copied together on one scroll, 'The Twelve'.
books.audience: The northern kingdom of Israel
books.setting: Bethel and Samaria at the height of Israel's prosperity under Jeroboam II
books.origin: Amos, a southerner, went north to Israel's royal sanctuary at Bethel, where the priest Amaziah told him to go home. A major earthquake around 760 BC, mentioned in his first verse, has left traces at Hazor and other sites.
books.description: Amos begins by condemning Israel's neighbours, then turns the same judgement on Israel for selling 'the poor for a pair of shoes', crushing the needy, and making worship a show. God hates their feasts: 'let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.' Five visions — locusts, fire, a plumbline, summer fruit and the Lord at the altar — show judgement coming. The book ends with the promise to raise up 'the tabernacle of David that is fallen'.

outline.title: Judgement on the nations — and on Israel
Five visions and the promise of restoration

key_verses.text: Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old:

books.christ: James quotes Amos 9:11-12 at the Jerusalem council: through Christ, David's fallen tabernacle is rebuilt and the Gentiles seek the Lord (Acts 15:16-17).

books.name: Obadiah
books.name_meaning: Named after Obadiah, 'servant of the LORD' — a common name; this prophet is otherwise unknown.
books.summary: The shortest book of the Old Testament: judgement on Edom for betraying its brother Judah, and the promise that 'the kingdom shall be the LORD's'.
books.author: Obadiah
books.author_note: Nothing is known of Obadiah beyond his name. Most date the book after Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Edom cheered and plundered. In the Hebrew Bible the twelve minor prophets were copied together on one scroll, 'The Twelve'.
books.audience: Judah, and indirectly Edom
books.setting: The aftermath of Jerusalem's fall
books.origin: Obadiah takes up the long feud between Jacob and Esau's descendants. Parts of it closely parallel Jeremiah 49:7-22.
books.description: Edom, secure in its mountain strongholds, is told its pride has deceived it: 'though thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I bring thee down.' Its crime was standing by, gloating and cutting off Judah's refugees on the day of disaster. 'As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee.' The Day of the LORD will restore Israel, and 'the kingdom shall be the LORD's'.

outline.title: The Day of the LORD and the kingdom

key_verses.text: Though thou exalt thyself as the eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I bring thee down, saith the LORD.
For the day of the LORD is near upon all the heathen: as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head.
And saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the LORD’S.

books.christ: The kingdom that 'shall be the LORD's' is the kingdom Christ proclaimed and will bring in full (Revelation 11:15).

books.name: Jonah
books.name_meaning: Named after Jonah son of Amittai; Jonah means 'dove'.
books.summary: A reluctant prophet runs from God, is swallowed by a great fish, preaches to Nineveh — and is angry when God spares it.
books.author: Unknown; about Jonah son of Amittai
books.author_note: The book tells Jonah's story in the third person. Jonah was a real prophet from Gath-hepher in the reign of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), and Jesus referred to him and to Nineveh's repentance (Matthew 12:39-41). In the Hebrew Bible the twelve minor prophets were copied together on one scroll, 'The Twelve'.
books.date: Events c. 780–750 BC; date of writing debated
books.audience: Israel
books.setting: Joppa, the Mediterranean Sea, and Nineveh, capital of Assyria
books.origin: Unlike the other prophets, Jonah is almost all narrative. It is read in synagogues on the afternoon of the Day of Atonement as a lesson in repentance and God's mercy.
books.description: Told to preach against Nineveh, Jonah sails the other way. God sends a storm; the sailors throw Jonah overboard, and a great fish swallows him. From inside it he prays: 'Salvation is of the LORD.' Given a second chance, he preaches, and the whole city repents in sackcloth. God relents — and Jonah sulks, because he knew God was 'gracious… and repentest thee of the evil'. The book ends with God's question about his compassion for Nineveh's people.

key_verses.text: But I will sacrifice unto thee with the voice of thanksgiving; I will pay that that I have vowed. Salvation is of the LORD.
And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.

And he prayed unto the LORD, and said, I pray thee, O LORD, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil.

books.christ: Jesus gave 'the sign of the prophet Jonas': as Jonah was three days in the fish, the Son of man would be three days in the earth (Matthew 12:40).

books.name: Micah
books.name_meaning: Named after Micah of Moresheth; Micah means 'Who is like the LORD?'
books.summary: A country prophet condemns corrupt leaders, names Bethlehem as the Messiah's birthplace, and sums up what God requires.
books.author: Micah the Morasthite
books.author_note: Micah came from Moresheth-gath in the Judean lowlands and prophesied under Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1), at the same time as Isaiah. A century later his words were quoted to save Jeremiah's life (Jeremiah 26:18). In the Hebrew Bible the twelve minor prophets were copied together on one scroll, 'The Twelve'.
books.audience: Samaria and Jerusalem
books.setting: Judah during the Assyrian threat
books.origin: Micah's oracles alternate between judgement and hope. Its promise of swords beaten into ploughshares (4:1-3) also appears in Isaiah 2.
books.description: Micah announces judgement on Samaria and Jerusalem for idolatry, land-grabbing and leaders who 'hate the good, and love the evil'. Yet he foresees nations streaming to the LORD's house and a ruler from Bethlehem Ephratah 'whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting'. God brings a case against his people and answers what he requires: 'to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.' It ends: 'Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity?'

outline.title: Corrupt leaders; the future king from Bethlehem
God's case against his people; hope in his mercy

key_verses.text: But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.

books.christ: When Herod asked where the Christ would be born, the scribes answered from Micah 5:2: Bethlehem (Matthew 2:5-6).

books.name: Nahum
books.name_meaning: Named after Nahum the Elkoshite; Nahum means 'comfort'.
books.summary: A poem announcing the fall of Nineveh, the cruel capital of Assyria — comfort for all it had oppressed.
books.author: Nahum the Elkoshite
books.author_note: Nothing is known of Nahum or the location of Elkosh. He cites the fall of Thebes (No-Amon, 3:8), which happened in 663 BC, so he wrote before Nineveh fell in 612 BC. In the Hebrew Bible the twelve minor prophets were copied together on one scroll, 'The Twelve'.
books.audience: Judah, suffering under Assyria
books.setting: The last decades of the Assyrian empire
books.origin: About a century after Jonah, Nineveh had returned to its violence. Nahum's vivid battle poetry describes its fall, which came when the Babylonians and Medes sacked it in 612 BC.
books.description: Nahum begins with the LORD as a jealous God who is 'slow to anger, and great in power' — yet 'good, a strong hold in the day of trouble'. He pictures the enemy chariots in Nineveh's streets and the city's gates opened by flood, and ends with a funeral song for 'the bloody city', whose fall makes everyone who hears of it clap their hands.

key_verses.text: The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.

books.christ: 'Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings' (1:15) is echoed in the gospel's 'beautiful feet' (Romans 10:15).

books.name: Habakkuk
books.name_meaning: Named after Habakkuk; the name probably means 'embrace'.
books.summary: A prophet questions God about injustice and learns that 'the just shall live by his faith', ending in a song of trust.
books.author: Habakkuk the prophet
books.author_note: Habakkuk is called 'the prophet' but nothing else is known of him. Chapter 3 carries musical notes, like a psalm. In the Hebrew Bible the twelve minor prophets were copied together on one scroll, 'The Twelve'.
books.audience: Judah, facing the rise of Babylon
books.setting: Judah shortly before the Babylonian invasions
books.origin: Habakkuk is a dialogue: the prophet speaks to God rather than to the people. A commentary on it (the Habakkuk Pesher) was among the first Dead Sea Scrolls found in 1947.
books.description: Habakkuk asks why God allows violence in Judah. God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans (Babylonians) to judge it. Habakkuk objects: how can God use a nation worse than Judah? He waits on his watchtower and is told to write the vision plainly: 'the just shall live by his faith', and the proud will fall. He ends with a prayer: even if the fig tree does not blossom and the fields yield nothing, 'yet I will rejoice in the LORD'.

outline.title: The just shall live by faith; woes on the proud

key_verses.text: Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.
For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
